en: Buddhist technical terms:
"Akṣara" (the syllable) is the *bimba* (reflexive image) devoid of emptiness (*tuccha-rūpa*) [which is] *nirvāṇa*, and [devoid of] cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
By means of the characteristic of perishable pleasure, the past untainted great bliss is imperishable; it is Akṣobhya.
(Seṭī, p.
70) It is unshakeable.
If the mind is empty of anything graspable and so forth, it is called Akṣobhya;
it is inconceivable. (Avasam, p. 29)
For that knowledge which is effortless is declared to be inconceivable; indeed,
that which is conceived as inconceivable cannot truly be inconceivable.
(Avataṃsaka Sūtra, 20, 30) What is this inconceivable realm? What is that inconceivable realm?
That element which is determined, not accessible to the mind, not measurable by the mind, and not to be realized through mental volition—
that is called the inconceivable element (*acintyadhātu*). And yet...
Furthermore, Blessed One, the mind itself is the inconceivable realm.
Why is that?
Because in a non-mind, no mind is found. It is certain.
For the mind is indeed [the Buddha], because of its awakening to reality as it is;
and yet, the inconceivable realm of the Blessed One possesses all aspects.
It is said elsewhere as well:
"O you whose intention is free from conceptual construction, whose mind is unestablished,
who are without memory or mental engagement, and who are without support— homage be to you!"
In the *Catuḥpradīpa*:
That which is born from conditions is indeed unborn;
for it has no arising by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
That which is dependent on conditions is said to be empty;
he who understands emptiness is heedful.

The empowerment of authorization (*anujñābhiṣeka*) is for the sake of the immeasurable realm of sentient beings, according to their respective inclinations, through the distinction between the conventional and the ultimate.
The seventh is the empowerment of authorization (*anujñābhiṣeka*), which brings about the perfection of Buddhahood for the purpose of teaching the most secret Vajrayāna.
Non-abiding nirvāṇa is that bliss located in the *uṣṇīṣa*, arising from dispassion— that is, from the departure of passion.
That [semen] is established;
however, that which has issued from the diamond-jewel is nirvāṇa.
This, moreover, is the King of Bliss.
Because he pervades the space between the *uṣṇīṣa* and the *vajramaṇi*, he is the one who has attained non-abiding nirvāṇa.
For this very reason, being preeminent, he is the Great Passion (*mahārāga*), the Immutable (*akṣara*), the Lord, and the Sovereign of the Three Realms. (Seṭī, p. 55)
The *śuddhakāya* (pure body), designated as the great bliss known as non-abiding nirvāṇa, is the consecration (*abhiṣeka*). (Seṭī, pp. 55–56)

Having explained the seven empowerments— which are of the nature of the lower conventional truth and serve as steps on the staircase to the palace of mundane and supramundane accomplishments— he [explains] the three empowerments known as the Vase, the Secret, and the Wisdom-Knowledge, which consist of the yogic conventional truth, are means for achieving mundane accomplishments, and are conducive to the ultimate truth.
He introduces [the topic] with the words beginning "Kumbha" (se ṭī, p.
21): regarding the term *amanasikāra*, many have fallen into disagreement.
Regarding this, someone says: "This is a corruption of language; in a compound, it ought to be *manaskāra*.
To this it is replied: because of the word "frequently" (*bahulam*) in the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam*.
When the compound is formed with the elision of the seventh case ending according to the rule "saptamyā aluk," we have *amanasikāraḥ* (non-mental attention) and *amanaskāraḥ*; likewise,
*tvacisāraḥ*.

"Tvaksāraḥ"; O Yudhiṣṭhira, these forms are thus established, and therefore this is not an incorrect word (*apaśabda*). Nor does the negative particle (*nañ*) here function as a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*).
Alternatively, non-existence (abhāva) must be expressed because it is the object [of the negation].
For in the case of "the king's wives are not to be seen by the sun" (*asūryampaśyā rājadārāḥ*), the non-existence of the sun is not what is intended;
rather, it is the seeing of the sun that would otherwise be applicable to the king's wives [which is here prohibited].

That has been refuted. In the same way, even in the case of "non-attention" (*amanasikāra*), it is the mental engagement (*manasikaraṇa*) with the grasped, the grasper, and so forth— which was previously established— that is refuted by the negative particle, not the mind itself.
Therefore, there is no fault.
Even in the case of the *paryudāsa* (exclusion) interpretation, there is no fault;
for when it is said, "Bring a non-Brahmin," the bringing of a Kṣatriya or similar person who resembles a Brahmin occurs.
But here too, the establishment of the experience of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) for heterogeneous things such as mats and the like has been made;
or rather, in this context, "mental attention" (*manasikāra*) is primarily characterized by the vowel *a*.
This is a compound with the middle term elided (*madhyamapadalopī samāsaḥ*), like the word *śākapārthiva* ("vegetable-king").
By this, the meaning is that whatever mental engagement there may be, it is entirely of the nature of non-arising.

The fact that the letter *a* acts as the non-producer of arising is stated in the *Hevajra Tantra*: "The letter *a* is the gateway to all phenomena, because they are unarisen from the very beginning," and so forth.
And in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*: "The letter *ā* is the foremost of all phonemes, of great significance, and the supreme syllable."
"For the Great Breath (mahāprāṇa) is indeed non-arising, devoid of verbal expression.
Alternatively: the letter *A* here is the seed-syllable of selflessness (*nairātmya*). And thus it is said in the *Hevajra*: "The beginning of *Āli* is the beginning of *Nairātmyā*."

By this, it is stated that all mental attention (*manasikāra*) is selfless and without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Or alternatively: "That wisdom (*dhī*) has been conceived by the Buddhas as having the intrinsic nature of the first vowel."
That very same Blessed Lady Prajñā [is realized] through the yoga of the stage of completion.

Alternatively: "a" is the term for luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), and "mental attention" (*manasikāra*) is the term for self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*). That which is both "a" and mental attention is "non-mental-attention" (*amanasikāra*).

By this term "non-mental engagement" (*amanasikāra*), the state of the inconceivable, luminous self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*)—the realization that carries the non-dual union of emptiness and compassion—is brought to completion. (Avaśaṃ, pp.
60–62) Amṛtakuṇḍalī.
Vidhnāntaka is Amṛtakuṇḍalī; his gaze is fixed upon the place of nectar, located at the forehead.
(Se tī pṛ 36-37)
But at the time of the *upasādhana*, the image (*bimba*) is Amṛtakuṇḍalī;
thus, by the name "Amṛtakuṇḍalī-bimba" in the terminology of the twilight language (*sandhyābhāṣā*).
It has been stated that this is wind (*vāyu*), and it is of five kinds. Thus, the Blessed One said in the *Samājottara*:
One should emit the breath consisting of the five jewels, empowered by the five Buddhas,
and visualize it in the form of a single mass at the tip of the nose.
Thus:

here, by the term "five jewels" (pañcaratna), one refers to the five elements beginning with earth, which possess the nature of the five mandalas of the tongue (rasanā); the breath consisting of these is "made of the five jewels," [referring] to the left nostril. Likewise:
The five Buddhas possess the nature of the five maṇḍalas of the *lalanā* and are the five aggregates beginning with consciousness;
the breath presided over by them is [inhaled] through the left nostril.
"Having emitted it in the form of a mass" means:
Here, "piṇḍa" refers to the state in which the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) within the central channel (*avadhūtī*), the *madhyamā*, is devoid of the nature of the left and right mandalas.
And having expelled that vital breath in the form of a "piṇḍa,"...
One should visualize [the breath] at the tip of the nose, from the pericarp into the middle of the pericarp,
not upon the petals of the lotus to the left or right.
Thus, the vital breath (prāṇa) is restrained in the form of a mass within the location of the point (bindu).
By that very [means], its retention (*dhāraṇā*) is described.
Thus, the secondary practice (*upasādhana*) is performed by means of the two limbs, namely, the form of the Amṛtakuṇḍalī.
(Se tī, pp. 41–42)
Regarding the three states,
there are three states therein;
the first is called the causal state (hetvavasthā).
From the initial arousal of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) until the arrival at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa).
The stage of fruition is the state consisting in the abandonment of all afflictions and the attainment [of all virtues] upon the arising of the knowledge of perfect awakening (samyaksaṃbodhi).
The stage of performing the welfare of sentient beings (*sattvārthakriyāvasthā*) begins from the first turning of the wheel of Dharma until the disappearance of the teaching.
Within that, the causal stage (*hetvavasthā*) is threefold: the stage of aspiration (*āśayāvasthā*),...
The stage of application and the stage of mastery;
therein, the stage of intention.
The vow for the non-liberation of sentient beings;
its causes are four, namely:
"The causes are spiritual lineage, a virtuous friend, compassion, and fearlessness toward suffering;
by these four conditions, the thought of awakening is generated.
Thus it is said.
In that regard, the stage of application is twofold: the perfections of one whose mind is characterized by resolute belief,
and those of one who practices with resolute belief.
There are ten perfections (*pāramitā*). For one who has attained the stages (*bhūmi*), the mind is endowed with four prosperities;
for that purpose, there are these seven perfections: generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, and skillful means.
For one who practices the conduct of resolute belief, there are ten perfections:
generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, aspiration, power, and knowledge; these are considered the ten perfections.

In that regard, the states of mastery are fivefold, known as the states of afflictions, rebirth, karma, means, and the ripening of sentient beings. Among these, one who abides in the causal state must perform all preliminary practices.

Furthermore, for one who abides in the state of fruition and the state of performing the welfare of sentient beings, initial activity proceeds spontaneously, as in the case of Śākyamuni. (Avatamsaka-sūtra, p.
11–12) The cultivation of the impure.
The body consists of a collection of feces, urine, semen, blood, phlegm, intestines, mucus, grease, exhaustion, the spleen, the liver, and so forth.
As it has been said:
"First, by means of your own intelligence, separate this leather bag [of the body] into its various parts."
With the sword of wisdom, sever the flesh from the skeleton.
"Even having separated the bones, look at the marrow within;
investigate for yourself whether there is any essence here. (Avasaṃ, p. 15)
The preliminary practice,
as it has been taught, must be performed by all yogins;
that which is intended as the gnosis for awakening is the indivisibility of emptiness and compassion.
The five perfections are designated by the term "initial action," yet it is not held that the perfection of wisdom is their essential nature or their hub.
The wise person who constantly and respectfully practices generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom becomes happy and remains in a state of well-being.
Generosity, ethical discipline, and patience are the causes for the Enjoyment Body and the Emanation Body;
meditative concentration and wisdom are the causes for the Dharma Body, while vigor is considered the cause for both.
( *Āvasaṃ*, p. 2) The joys (*ānanda*):
there are four joys—joy (*ānanda*),...
Supreme bliss, innate bliss, and the bliss of cessation.
Otherwise, that which was stated—“Having observed the target between the supreme [joy] and the cessation [of joy], make it firm”—would not be consistent. (Avaśyasaṃgrahaṇī, p. 23)
"From this moment forth, you are the consolation, liberated from all obscurations, and the pledge of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
Reassurance for the sake of awakening.
(Avatamsaka Sūtra, p.
38) Upāsaka.
Diligently engaged in the worship of the Buddha, resting in perfect tranquility,
one should be endowed with skillful means for the benefit of sentient beings. One should always avoid evil deeds and refrain from association with the most wicked.
Restraining a living being from evil, one should point out the sin in every instance.
Freed from all superimpositions, he is perfectly concentrated in meditative absorption at all times.
The wise one, possessing supreme bliss, shall accomplish awakening.
Who always exerts effort and maintains compassion; who, even through hardship, does not do what is undesirable, but performs the highest service?
Supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) refers to the ability to travel through space and other such feats. (AvaSaṃ, p. 10; SeTī, p. 47)
Action is the mental deliberation of body, speech, and mind (*avaśaṃ*, p.
32); physical action is deportment, and vocal action is the teaching of the Dharma.
The mental action of the wise one who is free from conceptual construction is the act of formal undertaking.
( *Avasāna-saṃgraha*, p. 54) The action-seal (*karmamudrā*) is the activity of body, speech, and mind.
The *mudrā* characterized by that [imagination] has the nature of conceptual construction;
within that *karmamudrā*—
Blisses arise there, differentiated according to the distinctions of moments;
from the knowledge of the moment, the knowledge of bliss is established in the syllable E-Vaṃ.

Therefore, having obtained the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), the fruit of non-movement arises; non-movement is movement that resembles [it]. How can the artificial illusion produced by the action-seal become non-artificial?
The wisdom known as the co-emergent (*sahaja*) arises.
It is the lotus, a mine of jewels consisting of the mass of bliss of the *karmāṅganā*.
That clear abode, through the union of the essences of the *bola* and *kakkola*, contains the conventional bodhicitta within the *avadhūtī*.
When that occurs, then another knowledge called "momentary" (kṣaṇika) and known as "innate" (sahaja) arises.
That is not the innate, motionless [state].
In its own nature,
it consists of the triad of wisdom, gnosis, and bliss, accompanied by the four moments during initiation.
And in Haṭhayoga, the fruit of the *karmamudrā* is said to be *niṣpanda*.
(AVS, p.
32–33) By means of the *karmamudrā*, there is the state of leaking bliss (*kṣarasukha*). (ST, p. 62)
The six vase empowerments are characterized by the water, crown, vajra, bell, name, and master empowerments.
Because all of these involve the operation of the vase, they are designated as the "Vase Empowerment" (*kalaśābhiṣeka*).
Furthermore, these are "empowerments of non-retrogression" because they possess the nature of the six Tathāgatas.
For instance, there is the Water Empowerment (*udakābhiṣeka*).
The mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna) is the nature of Akṣobhya;
the crown consecration (mukuṭābhiṣeka) is the nature of Ratnasambhava, consisting of the wisdom of equality (samatājñāna);
and the vajra consecration (vajrābhiṣeka) is the nature of Amitābha, consisting of the wisdom of discernment (pratyavekṣaṇājñāna).
The empowerment of sovereignty (adhipatyābhiṣeka) has the nature of Amoghasiddhi, consisting of the performance of activities (kṛtyānuṣṭhāna).

The name empowerment (nāmābhiṣeka) consists of the wisdom of the pure dharmadhātu accompanied by knowledge through the cessation of ignorance, and is the very form of Vairocana. The master empowerment (ācāryābhiṣeka), however, has the nature of immutable gnosis (akṣarajñāna).
And here there are five consecrations, because of the activity of the vidyās such as Locanā and the others within those five. And here,
for the purpose of washing away the stains of ignorance, by means of the Vajrācārya in the form of Akṣobhya, [the rite is performed] upon the disciple who has taken recourse to the form of Vairocana.
The sprinkling with water should be given.
Likewise, in all cases, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) which is the future state of Buddhahood, having become the crown-protrusion (uṣṇīṣa) of the mindless, is the crown consecration (mukuṭābhiṣeka).
Observing the ritual procedure for the Vajra-consecration as if to establish the seed of indivisible gnosis,

likewise the Vajra-bell— by means of the previous intention— is twelve finger-widths in measure; with its face turned downward, it is intended to demonstrate that the nature of all phenomena is the nature of the union of the lotus and the vajra, and to awaken [the practitioner] to the fact that the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) is the expression of indivisible gnosis.
On the upper and lower parts of the head, there is a double garland of vajra-rows.
Then, one should perform the consecration with this resounding vajra-bell;
for it is here, through the awakening to all unsurpassed phenomena, that the bell manifests its transformative power in order to proclaim its preeminence.
And for the purpose of demonstrating causality, the bestowal of the vajra initiation occurs first, even bypassing the vajra-bhaṇṭa initiation which serves as its cause;
this is for the sake of establishing that "all phenomena are nameless," and for the purpose of providing the introductory narrative for the name appropriate to the future Lord of Munis.
And there is the name-consecration (*nāmābhiṣeka*), which involves the removal of one's former name and the conferring of a new name according to the family and lineage of one’s own deity;

as well as the master-consecration (*ācāryābhiṣeka*), characterized by the commitments (*samaya*) of the vajra, the bell, and the mudrā, the authorization regarding fitness, the declaration of the vow (*vrata*), and the granting of encouragement (*āśvāsa*).
The four bodies constitute the *dharmakāya* because they have the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) Tathāgata as their essence. (Avatamsaka-sūtra, pp. 36–38)
It is the *saṃbhogakāya* because it consists of mere appearance;
it is the *nirmāṇakāya* because it is the imagined and emanated body;
and it is the *svābhāvikakāya* because it is the single flavor of the three bodies.
As it has been said:
"The unconditioned mind and its phenomena are characterized by enjoyment;
that very [mind] is the manifold emanation, the seed of all intrinsic natures."
For this very reason, they call the body the support of the dharmas the *dharmakāya*.

Therefore, the Dharmakāya is precisely the body of union (*yuganaddhakāya*), distinct from both the Enjoyment Body (*sāmbhogikakāya*) and the Essential Body (*svābhāvikakāya*), and is to be personally realized by yogins. (Seṭī, p.
57) [The moments].

There are four moments: the variegated (*vicitra*), the ripening (*vipāka*), the distinctive (*vilakṣaṇa*), and the crushing (*vimarda*). In the context of consecration (*seka*), one should understand that the distinctive moment is placed in the middle.
In Haṭhayoga, however, it is at the end of the innate (*sahaja*) and the distinctive moments.
The state of stability is to be understood;
and this was taught by the Blessed One regarding the yoga of consecration and forceful methods (*sekahaṭhayoga*) in the *Avaśyakasamuccaya* (p.
Patience and patience consist in enduring blows from cruel, heated saws and the like. (Avataṃsakasūtra, p. 3)

The secret consecration (*guhyābhiṣeka*) is the bestowal of the bodhicitta produced by both [the master and the disciple] at the same time, for the purpose of making wisdom and faith into a field and for the purpose of guarding the commitments (*samaya*).
The etymological derivation is: "you illuminate by means of both wisdom and secret skillful means" (*prajñopāyaguhyābhyāṃ dīpayati*).
The commitment of the bell (*ghaṇṭāsamaya*) is:
"you are beyond the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma. (AVS, p. 38)
The bell-samaya is for the purpose of instruction.
(Avasam, p.
38) This is the fourth consecration.
Some say that the fourth object of realization is that which is to be accomplished by means of the seven limbs characterized by the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*).
This very knowledge of wisdom, when practiced, is like the stainless autumn sky.
Others say that the fourth meaning is as follows:
the very gnosis of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*), which is the nature of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), whose essence is the arising of primordial matter,
and whose pure intrinsic nature flows as the non-dual union (*yuganaddha*), is the fourth meaning— so say others.
And other alternative positions are not stated here for fear of prolixity. (Avatārasaṃgraha, p. 39)
The four divine abidings consist of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which takes the form of affection for all sentient beings as if they were one's only son;
and compassion (*karuṇā*), whose nature is the longing to rescue [beings] from the ocean of saṃsāra, both from suffering itself and from the causes of suffering.
Having cultivated compassion, joy arising from a mind overflowing with the taking of refuge in the Three Jewels, and equanimity characterized by the absence of attachment (Avatārasaṃgraha, pp. 4–5).
The world is inseparable from emptiness and compassion;
consisting of cause and effect, it is merely the single flavor of cyclic existence and nirvāṇa. (Avataṃsaka Sūtra, p. 26)
The world. (Avaśaṃsā, p. 42) The knowledge-mudrā is the knowledge-mudrā conceptualized by one's own mind.
The nature of the goddesses beginning with Viśvamātā; that is to say, as previously stated.
(Seṭī, p. 56)

The state of vibrating bliss (*spandasukha*) is attained through the *jñānamudrā*. The term "vibration" (*spanda*) includes the imperishable (*akṣara*) as well, due to its similarity to emission (*srāva*).
These two [are known as] the perishable (*kṣara*) and the vibration (*spanda*).
When the state of bliss has been directly realized, it serves as the means for accomplishing mundane siddhis characterized by mastery over the desire and form realms.
(Seṭī, p. 62) [The Verses on the Three Refuges]
Homage to the Buddha, the Teacher; homage to the Dharma, the Protector;
homage to the great Saṅgha—homage perpetually to all three.
The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds;
I rejoice in the merit of the world; and I fix my mind upon the enlightenment of a Buddha.
Until enlightenment, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Supreme Assembly;
I generate the mind of awakening for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of myself and others.
I generate the supreme mind of enlightenment; I invite all sentient beings. I shall practice the desired, sublime conduct of enlightenment; may I become a Buddha.
For the benefit of the world.
I shall confess all evils, rejoice in all merits,
and observe the noble eightfold *poṣadha* fast that has been undertaken.
The Dharma-seal,
the Dharma-seal, whose nature is the Dharmadhātu, is free from conceptual proliferation.
Non-conceptual, uncontrived, devoid of arising, and having compassion as its intrinsic nature, it is the supreme means, uniquely beautiful through its singular bliss.

That which is distinct from wisdom (*prajñā*), whose nature is coemergent (*sahaja*) due to its continuous flow, because of its own coemergent arising, is designated as the "Dharma-seal" (*dharmamudrā*).
Its other characteristic, which resembles the rays of the sun for crossing the darkness of confused ignorance,

should be understood through the instruction of the Guru as being devoid of even the slightest thorn of delusion, such as a blade of grass or a husk. It is entirely free from the great agitation caused by earth, water, wind, and fire.
One should understand that it is the unique nature of the three worlds, and that it is indivisible from waveless emptiness and compassion.
Lalanā, Rasanā,
and Avadhūtī, who dwells in the space between them.
That very [reality] is the *dharmamudrā*, because it is the single mental state whose innate nature is all objects of knowledge realized through the instruction of a true guru,
being non-different from the *mahāmudrā*.
It is the cause. (Avasāna, pp.
33–34) The source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) is as follows: the Blessed Buddha, the perfectly awakened one, is born from the syllable *A*.
The letter A is the foremost of all phonemes, of great significance, and the supreme syllable;
it is indeed the great vital breath, unarisen, and devoid of verbal expression.
That from which the arising of all qualities such as sovereignty occurs for the Buddhas is called Dharmodaya; it is supreme, consisting of merit and gnosis.
Meditation and meditation [are so called] because they proceed spontaneously and effortlessly, following the nature of all things.
(The *Avaśyaka-saṃgrahaṇī*, p. 55): "The moon having vanished" means that the sixteenth digit of the sun has gone to the *uṣṇīṣa*-lotus; thus, the moon has vanished.
Thus it is declared:
the name-consecration (*nāmābhiṣeka*) is [performed] with the intention that the castes, such as Brāhmaṇas and others, are of a single essence, [addressing him as] "Amukavajra. (Seṭī, p. 55)

Thus, because of the naming [of the disciple] through the fulfillment of the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and by virtue of the perpetual prevention of the purification of passion, hatred, and so forth, this is the sixth, the Name Empowerment (*nāmābhiṣeka*). (Seṭī, p. 21) This is the sign (*nimitta*).
Furthermore,
another six signs, beginning with the flame and ending with the drop, were taught by the Blessed One in the *Māyājāla* in the chapter on meditative absorption (*samādhi*). They are as follows:
Born from space, self-existent, the great fire of the wisdom of insight;
Vairocana of great radiance, the illuminator of the light of gnosis.
The lamp of the world, the torch of knowledge, of great splendor and luminous;
the fierce King of Vidyās, the Lord of Mantras, the King of Mantras who accomplishes the great purpose.
Thus, with these two verses, the Blessed One has spoken of the subsequent sign (*aparanimitta*) in the *Māyājāla* by means of intentional language (*sandhyābhāṣā*).
From the previously mentioned cloudless sky, there arises a manifestation.
He who is that self-arisen one born from space, because his mind is free from all conceptual constructions;
herein lies the fire of the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*).
The appearance of flames;

Vairocana, the great radiance—this is the appearance of the moon. That very same [Vairocana], as the manifestation of the light of gnosis and the illuminator, is the appearance of the sun, the lamp of the world.
"The torch of knowledge" is the appearance of Rāhu;
"of great brilliance and luminous" is the appearance of lightning.
"The King of Vidyās, the Lord of Fierce Mantras" refers to the appearance of the *bindu* in the form of a blue-colored lunar disc.

"The King of Mantras, the accomplisher of the Great Purpose" means that the appearance of all phenomena (*bhāva*) of the three realms in all their aspects is seen by the yogin through the operation of the eyes and other sense faculties as being equal to the appearances of an illusion or a dream. (Seṭī, pp. 40–41)
Having attained the action-seal (karmamudrā), the fruit of non-vibration arises;
non-vibration is a vibration that is similar [to itself].
That is not the innate (sahaja) quiescence (niṣpanda), but rather something resembling the innate;
it is by way of its own nature.
In the initiation, the triad of blisses—wisdom, gnosis, and supreme bliss—is associated with the four moments;
and in Haṭhayoga, the fruit of the motionless (*niṣpanda*) is said to result from the action-seal (*karmamudrā*). (AVS, pp. 32–33)
The five knowledges are characterized as the mirror-like, the equality, the discerning, the all-accomplishing, and the perfectly pure dharma-realm. (Avataṃsaka, p. 37)
The five Tathāgatas,

on a ground consecrated by a maṇḍala, having fashioned a desired small maṇḍala— square or one of the other four shapes— in its center, upon a solar disc at the heart of a multicolored eight-petaled lotus, [they appear] as the blue syllable *HŪṂ* fully perfected.
Akṣobhya is black in color and holds the earth-touching mudrā (bhūsparśamudrā).
Following that, on the eastern petal is Vairocana, white in color, produced from the white syllable Oṃ, and holding the bodhyaṅgī mudrā.
Then, on the southern petal, [is] Ratnasambhava, yellow in color, born from a yellow syllable TRĀṂ, and holding the gesture of granting boons (varadamudrā);
then, on the western petal, [is the one] produced from a red syllable HRĪṂ.
Having meditated on Amitābha, red in color, holding the samādhi-mudrā,
and on Amoghasiddhi in the northern petal, green in color, born from the syllable Khaṃ, holding the abhaya-mudrā; and having meditated [on them].
These five Tathāgatas are clothed in saffron robes, wear ushnishas, have their heads and faces shaven, and stand upon solar discs;
Vairocana alone stands upon a lunar disc.
Then the four [Buddhas] face Akṣobhya, while Akṣobhya faces the practitioner. (Avasam, p.
5) [The ten] Pāramitās.
Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means,
aspiration, power, and knowledge are considered the ten perfections.
( *Avatārasaṃgraha*, p. 12) "Full" means the removal and departure of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the obscurations of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obscurations to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Thus, it is designated by the word "full" (pūrṇa).
There is no cutting off of knowledge, nor is there a filling of it.
As it has been said in the Āgama:
But for the Buddhas it is eternally arisen, not for those whose minds are defiled by ignorance.
And by the venerable Saraha:
Victorious is the one King of Bliss, who is without cause, eternally arisen for the worlds,
at the very moment of whose description [the Buddha] became impoverished of words.
The Omniscient One.
That which is the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) of the bodhicitta is called *pūrṇā*.
This very state is what must be stabilized by the practitioners of yoga.
For this moon of bliss, once stabilized through the full breath-retention (*pūrṇāyāma*), arises and perishes again and again. (Seṭī, p.
64) The gift of the *poṣadha*.
First is the giving of the *poṣadha*:
"Pay attention, Venerable Teacher! I, named so-and-so..."
"I, a lay follower, go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, until I reach the seat of enlightenment. Thus, three times and again three times.
"May you remember me as one who has thus gone for refuge to the Three Jewels."
Pay heed,
O Teacher! I, the lay follower named so-and-so,
from this moment until tomorrow at sunrise, during this interval, [abstain] from the killing of any living being.
From the seizing of another's property, from unchastity,
and from the utterance of divisive speech which generates the fault of falsehood;
From drinking [intoxicants], from eating at improper times, and from [the use of] garlands, cosmetics, dancing, singing, and perfumes.
"Today I have desisted from eating meat from a slaughtered bird; for that duration, I shall observe [the precepts] through these eight qualities. The *Poṣadha-gāthā* states:
'The confession of all misdeeds and the rejoicing in all merits... (Avadānaśataka, pp. 3–4). [The verse continues: "...and the rejoicing in all merits."
Having observed the fast, I shall practice the noble eightfold poṣadha.
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is the cognition of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, free from the grasped and the grasper.
And wisdom consists in the realization characterized by the non-apprehension of all phenomena. (Avataṃsaka-sūtra, p. 3)

In this context, the intellect (*buddhi*) which maintains the forms of the grasped and the grasper consists of the four elements and the five aggregates; wisdom (*prajñā*) has as its nature the woman who is composed of the six objects. Wisdom is manifold, it is the fruition, it is the crushing, and it is characterized by distinctness. (Avatārasaṃgraha, p. 39) Wisdom is variegated, it is the maturation, it is the destruction, and it is of a different character.
Therefore, know its true nature, by which you are the sovereign lord of the world.
Wisdom is existence, and it is equal; it is the three bodies and the three vehicles.
That very thing is the practice, the skillful means for bliss, and that, O Yogins, is my supreme state.
Mañjuvajra, Mahāmāyā, Vajraḍāka, and others likewise—wisdom alone appears through differentiation; that very logic is the essence of the Victorious Ones.
When one has realized that the mind has departed, being without support, unsurpassed,
peaceful, pure, and without appearance— this awareness is proclaimed as wisdom (prajñā).
( *Avasāṃ*, p. 52) Regarding the term *prajñājñānābhiṣeka* (the consecration of wisdom-knowledge), there are two etymological derivations for *prajñājñāna*: [first,] by means of *prajñā*...
Knowledge (*jñāna*) is indeed wisdom (*prajñā*), which is external knowledge.

In that context, wisdom (*prajñā*) is the intellect (*buddhi*) that assumes the forms of the grasped and the grasper; it consists of the four elements and five aggregates, and has as its nature the woman who is composed of the six sense-objects.
The prior etymological derivation is that the knowledge of the *bodhicitta* arises from that [wisdom] which serves as its causal basis.
That very [consciousness] devoid of the two aspects is "vijñāna"—this is another etymological derivation.
(Avaśaṃ, pp. 38–39). Prāṇāyāma.
What is called *prāṇāyāma* is the cessation of the flow through the left and right channels, *lalanā* and *rasanā*.
It is the constant movement of the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*) within the central portion of the *avadhūtī*.

Through the yoga of inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*), one performs inhalation with the syllable *oṃ*, retention with the syllable *hūṃ*, and [exhalation] with the syllable *āḥ* within the *avadhūtī*.
"The yogi performs exhalation with the nature of the moon, sun, and Rāhu"—this is the limb of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). (Seṭī, pp.

38–39) [The topics include] the authorization of fitness (*bhavyatānujñā*), the reality of the mandala (*maṇḍalatattva*), and the characteristic of the purification of the mandala (*maṇḍalaviśuddhilakṣaṇa*).
The reality of the deity, characterized by the purity of the deity, the preparation of the preceptor, the knowledge for accomplishing the mandala,
the five lamps, the consumption of nectar, the reality of fitness, and the absence of intrinsic nature— these,
from the perspective of the generation stage (utpannakrama)—

The permission for the turning of the wheel of Dharma (the permission regarding capacity). (Avataṃsaka Sūtra, p. 38) "Phenomena" (bhāva) refers to those things that come into being from causes and conditions.
The cultivation of all entities, whether stable or moving, such as the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases. (Seṭī, p. 59)
The cultivation of body is at the forehead; the cultivation of speech is at the heart; the cultivation of mind is at the secret place.
The collection of the drops (*bindu*) of the body and so forth is their unification within the *vajramaṇi*;
therein, the cultivation of gnosis (*jñāna-bhāvanā*) is the mandala. (Seṭī, p. 62)
The maṇḍala is said to be the essence, the bodhicitta of great bliss;
because it performs the act of grasping, it is considered a maṇḍala, which is [derived from] the root *mal* (to grind/grasp).
The recitation of mantra: what is called the recitation of mantra is the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇasaṃyama*). (Seṭī, p. 43) The Mahāmudrā.
And this is a great seal (mudrā), thus it is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā).
The Great Seal is devoid of intrinsic nature,
free from the obscurations of knowledge and the knowable, and resembles the stainless autumn sky at midday.
She is the support for all prosperity, whose sole nature is both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, whose body is non-referential compassion,
and whose sole nature is great bliss.
By means of that Mahāmudrā, whose nature is inconceivable, the fruit known as Samayamudrā is attained.
It is born. (Avasāna-saṃgraha, pp. 34–35) This is both great and a seal; thus it is the Mahāmudrā. Its greatness—
Furthermore, this [Mahāmudrā] is endowed with the excellence of all aspects and is not merely partial;
the Result-Seal (phalamudrā), however, is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā).
Its greatness consists in the greatness of abandonment and the greatness of realization.

In this context, the greatness of abandonment (*prahāṇa-mahattva*) is characterized by the direct realization of the luminosity known as the natural state, which has the characteristic of abandoning all obscurations and all stains. The greatness of realization (*adhigama-mahattva*), however, has as its essential nature the direct realization of the body known as the "unified pair" (*yuganaddha*), which consists of all perfectly pure Buddhas.

The meditation on the unchanging syllable (*niṣpandākṣara*) by means of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), however, is the means for accomplishing supramundane siddhi, which is characterized by omniscience (*sarvajñatva*). (Seṭī, p. 56–57; Seṭī, p. 62)
She is called *mudrā* because she bestows joy (*muda*), that is, a specific bliss and delight;
she perpetually maintains this joy, characterized by the knowledge of supreme immutable bliss, from its previous state.
"By means of the yoga of immovability" refers to the *mudrā*. (Seṭī, p.
56) This is to declare that the *mudrā-samaya* is one's own nature as the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).
The seal-commitment (*mudrā-samaya*); the body of union (*yuganaddha-kāya*) and indeed the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

The host of deities to be supported— such as Vairocana and others— who consist of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) and so forth, which are pure and luminous by nature as the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*),
as well as the supporting mandala such as the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*),
are precisely what constitute the supramundane mandala in all the kings of tantras.

It is sung: because it has the nature of all the qualities of a Buddha, this very [state] whose nature is the non-duality of the two truths is called "Yuganaddha" (the Union). Therefore, it is the Yuganaddhakāya.
Thus, the *dharmakāya* is distinct from both the *sāmbhogika* and *svābhāvika* [kāyas], and is to be personally realized by the yogi. (Seṭī, p.
57) Regarding the four limbs of yoga: *sevā* is so called because it is served—that is, practiced—by those seeking liberation.
The limb of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the limb of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) extend up to the vision of the images of smoke and so forth.
That indeed is the supreme service (*sevā*), which must be performed by means of the nectar of knowledge, namely through the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) alone. (Seṭī, p. 36)
The cultivation of the signs beginning with smoke is *sevā* (service). (Seṭī, p.
36) At the time of *sevā*, one should diligently visualize the form of Mahoṣṇīṣa;
however, at the time of *upasādhana*, one visualizes the form of Amṛtakuṇḍalī.
One intent on yoga should meditate upon the form of the deity during the *sādhana*;
however, at the time of the *mahāsādhana*, one should meditate upon the all-pervading Lord Buddha as the image.
(Seṭī, p.
39) Here, by means of another intentional language (*sandhyābhāṣā*), the uṣṇīṣa-image is the Buddha-image, [pervading] the three realms without exception.

Having established the mind-vajra in the space of the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), one should meditate upon it during the stage of service—at the first stage—by means of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and stabilize it by means of the limb of meditation (*dhyānāṅga*).
(Seṭī, p. 39)
Thus, through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), the limb of service (*sevāṅga*) is described.
By the term "the form of Amṛtakuṇḍalī," or in the terminology of the twilight language (*sandhyābhāṣā*), the vital wind (*vāyu*) is expressed.
Thus, the vital breath (prāṇa) is restrained in the form of a mass at the location of the drop (bindu);
by that very means, its retention (dhāraṇā) is defined.

Thus, the secondary practice (*upasādhana*) is performed by means of the form of Amṛtakuṇḍalī through two limbs. That very secondary practice is called the "vajra-recitation" (*vajrajāpa*). It is also called the secondary practice of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and concentration (*dhāraṇā*). (Seṭī, pp. 41–42)
The means of accomplishment is the image of the deity within the practice;
here, by the power of concentration (*dhāraṇā*), [one visualizes] that which resides at the navel.

The yogi perceives Caṇḍālī as blazing, free from all obscurations, resembling a reflected image (*pratisenā*), emitting clouds of infinite rays of light from the Buddhas, and resplendent with a circle of radiance.
He describes that recollection (*anusmṛti*) as the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). (Seṭī, p. 42)
The rule is that at the conclusion of the dhāraṇā, the yogin should meditate upon Caṇḍālī during the Great Accomplishment (mahāsādhana).
Then, by the flame of her gnosis, the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth are incinerated and become unified as a single mass.

The consciousnesses and the elements, such as earth, which reside in the left and right channels and possess the nature of the maṇḍalas, enter the moon-maṇḍala in the forehead. Then, when the moon has been melted by the flame of gnosis from the Caṇḍālī, that bodhicitta descends in the form of a drop.
In the throat, heart, navel, and the secret lotus, by way of the natures of bliss, supreme bliss, and the cessation-bliss;
then, up to the vajra-jewel, by way of the nature of innate bliss.

Alternatively, by means of its own nature—which is distinct from the crushing of various ripened karmic results—it bestows bliss within the jewel when it is full of the sixteen digits through the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). The phrase "resembling sexual union" (*surata*) is merely an illustration; [the bliss] is [superior] by its very essence.
The pleasure born of the two organs does not equal even a thousand-millionth part of the supreme immutable pleasure (*paramākṣarasukha*).
Here, that state of immutable pleasure which consists of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) is an indescribable state, unknown to child-like yogins. It...

For Bodhisattvas, this is called the "samādhi of emptiness," and it does not, however, follow the meaning of nihilism according to worldly convention. Thus, through the yoga of the six limbs, Buddhahood is accomplished for yogins. (Seṭī, p. 42) The yogi...
Yoga is the six-limbed yoga that has reached the ultimate limit of excellence;
those who possess that yoga are yogins who have attained the state of the Great Vajradhara.
(Vajra-ṭīkā, p. 60): Just as with the Akṣobhya-mudrā, the Vajra is the primary gnosis, while the others are secondary.
Likewise, by means of the Vajrasattva-mudrā, consciousness (vijñāna) would also be the back [of the hand], and the primary [element] would be the vajra.
And it is said in the *Vajraśekhara*:
Firm, possessing gentleness and amiability, characterized by being uncuttable and unbreakable, neither burning nor subject to destruction—this is called the emptiness-vajra. (Avataṃsaka-sūtra, p.
32, 37) By means of the measure of twelve finger-breadths, it represents the purity of the twelvefold dependent origination.
The *vajra* is "indestructible," as stated in the *Hevajra*: (*Abhisamayamañjarī*, p.

37). The *vajra-bell* (*vajraghaṇṭā*)—according to the previous intention—is also twelve finger-breadths in measurement, with its face turned downward, and is characterized by the state of non-self-nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) through the meditative union (*samāpatti*) of the lotus and the *vajra*.

To establish the intrinsic nature of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-svabhāva*) and to awaken one to the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) as being the expression of indivisible gnosis, there is a pair of vajra-garland ornaments shining above and below the head. (Avaśaṃ, p.
37) This is the vajra-recitation (*vajrajāpa*).
"Prāṇāyāma" and "vajrajāpa" are to be recited as limbs inseparable from the middle [channel]. (Seṭī, p.
33) That very [practice] is called the "subsidiary sādhana" (upasādhana), namely, vajrajāpa. (Seṭī, p. 42)
Vajradhātvīśvarī is among these [Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍaravāsinī, and Tāriṇī],
possessing the nature of Āli and having the form of Vajrasattva.
The Sovereign Lady of the Vajra Realm is the Leader.
She alone is designated as the Blessed One, Suchness, Emptiness, the Perfection of Wisdom, the Limit of Reality, and Selflessness. (Avaśaṃ, p. 43)

The Vajra-vow initiation (*vajravratābhiṣeka*) is the complete purification of the sense objects such as form and the sense faculties such as the eyes; it is called the fifth initiation, the Vajra-vow initiation, because by means of the restraint of ordinary objects, it brings about the attainment of the siddhi of Mahāmudrā. (Seṭī, p. 21)

The Vajra-samaya is so called because it serves to awaken [the disciple] with the thought: "From this moment forth, you are the unconditioned Vajra-samaya, the dharma of awakening that flows through the two-fold union. (Avatāra-saṃgraha, p. 38)
Vajrasattva:
by "vajra" emptiness is expressed, and by "sattva" mere gnosis.
The identity of these two is established through the nature of Vajrasattva.
The distinction between emptiness and compassion is like that between a lamp and its light;
the unity of emptiness and compassion is like that between a lamp and its light.
Emptiness is not other than phenomena, nor do phenomena exist without it;
they are inseparable, just like the relationship between the produced and the impermanent.
The universal form [is perceived] by means of the two eyes half-opened through the suspension of the gaze within the space between [the eyebrows].
In the empty sky, devoid of subject and object, that which is not mentally constructed— a reflection directly perceived by the yogi like a dream—
that reflection is the universal reflection (*viśvabimba*).
This is vigor (*vīrya*).
And diligence [is attained] by enduring the affliction of the eight worldly dharmas;
the vow-proclamation is for the purpose of rejecting external vows, and the vajra-vow is for the purpose of indicating that the earth and so forth have the nature of [the five elements].
The grammatical derivation is as follows:
for "bhūḥ" is the own-nature (*svarūpa*) of the earth and so forth; thus, "bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ" means "may [the earth] become. (Avaśyakasamuccaya-bhāṣya, p.
He practiced the conduct after having performed the gift of his body;
for it is said: "Having given the gift of his body, one should thereafter undertake the practice" (He Ta 1).
Because of the statement [in the *Avaśyaka-niryukti*, verse 619]:
"Giving and conduct last until the end of the body; [only] tranquility [lasts beyond]."
It is free from the transformations of the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*). (Seṭī, p.
60) Morality (*śīla*) is so called because it restrains body, speech, and mind for the sake of all sentient beings.
Pure, meaning untouched by the stains of the afflictions (*kleśa*). (Svavṛtti, p. 3; Sphuṭārthā, p. 60)
The pure body is the pure body known as great bliss, which is called non-abiding nirvāṇa.
That which is the body-bindu (kāyabindu) as the reverse of the pure body known as great bliss is the pure body due to the exhaustion of the fourth state.
From the pure body [arise] the dharma, enjoyment, and emanation bodies.
They flash forth. (Seṭī, pp.
55–56) "Empty" [means] because at the end of the death of living beings, there is the relinquishing of the aggregates and the grasping of the aggregates belonging to the portion of rebirth.
That intermediate state, which is the single characteristic of emptiness and the vision of the three worlds, is called "emptiness.
Emptiness has the characteristic of being endowed with the excellence of all aspects.
The six perfections are as follows: generosity is cow dung mixed with water; ethical discipline is sweeping; and patience is—
The removal of small ants is vigor; the stabilization of the ritual action is meditative concentration; making the mind one-pointed at that very moment is wisdom, radiant with excellent lines.
Having constructed the maṇḍala of the Sage, one obtains these very six perfections.
He becomes golden-hued, liberated from all diseases, distinguished among gods and men, with a radiant splendor like the moon;
he is born into a royal lineage, enriched with wealth and gold.
Having performed physical deeds within this supreme abode of the Sugata,
The *samayamudrā* has the nature of the forms of the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*, appearing in a translucent form.
And that which is the radiation of Vajradhara in the form of Heruka for the sake of sentient beings is designated as the *samayamudrā*.
Having taken up that *samayamudrā*, it is fivefold in the form of a wheel.
Having conceptualized fivefold gnosis through the mirror-like, the equality, the discerning, the all-accomplishing,

and the utterly pure dharmadhātu [gnoses], by means of the yoga of the initial union, the yoga of the glory of the king of the maṇḍala, the yoga of the glory of the king of action, the yoga of the drop, and the subtle yoga.
The masters meditate upon the assembly of the samaya-mudrās; [this is] the *samāja*. (Avaśaṃ, p. 35) *Samāja* means an assembly.
"In brief, the mind has the form of the assembly" means that, in brief, because all phenomena have a single form— namely, the form of great bliss— the mind, which is the bodhicitta,
has the form of the assembly.
Knowledge that takes the form of the initiation of the Dharma-mudrā and Mahā-mudrā is truly designated as *samāja* (assembly). (*Abhisamayamañjarī*, p.
35) This is the superimposition (*samāropa*).
The meditation on Mahāmudrā, unmarked by the stains of all conceptual constructions, is the superimposition; it is the innate (*sahaja*). (Seṭī, p. 483)
Everything that is innate is designated as "innate" because it conforms to the shadow of the innate; that is,
the shadow of the innate conveys a cognition similar to the innate.
The innate is the gnosis of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*).
For this very reason, there is no arising of the innate from that gnosis of wisdom,
because it is innate.
The "name" (*nāma*) is the uncontrived intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of all phenomena— that is to say, their specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
The teachers, out of their skillfulness...

Thinking that they have attained the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*) and experienced the co-emergent (*sahaja*), they give rise to satisfaction; and being satisfied, they do not even know the report of the Dharma-seal (*dharmamudrā*). Not knowing the Dharma-seal, how can they [attain] that which is uncontrived by means of the contrived action-seal (*karmamudrā*) alone?
The gnosis known as the co-emergent (sahaja) arises;
for from a cause of the same nature, an effect of that very same nature is produced.
But it does not arise from a heterogeneous cause; just as a rice sprout arises from a rice seed,
but not from *kodrava* grain.
Likewise, from the uncontrived *dharmamudrā*, the uncontrived innate (*sahaja*) arises;
[it is] the jewel-mine of the mass of blisses of the *karmāṅganā*.

The lotus is that clear abode; when it becomes filled with the *saṃvṛti-bodhicitta* (conventional bodhicitta) within the jewel [of the urethra] through the union of the fluids of the *bola* and *kakkola* by means of the *avadhūtī*,
it is known by another name, "the momentary" (*kṣaṇika*).
The gnosis known as the co-emergent (*sahaja*) arises. The body of the co-emergent is the internal *vidyā*, the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), which is luminous by nature.
Mahāmudrā, whose nature is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), is the state of fullness that is the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the *dharmadhātu*; she is called the Innate Body (*sahajatanu*).
(Seṭī, p. 69) The drop (*bindu*) becomes empty.
And that [syllable], being free from the two extremes, is called the supreme syllable (paramākṣara);
the supreme syllable is also the letter A.
The Perfectly Awakened One, born from the letter *A*, whose nature consists of wisdom and skillful means, is Vajrasattva; he is called the neuter state and the Innate Body (*sahajakāya*).
And that Blessed One Kālacakra is the supreme immutable, the state of bliss. (Seṭī, p. 69)
Similarity is similarity; for example, the reflection of a face cast in a mirror is not the face itself.
There was no prior accomplishment, nor is there accomplishment now;
that very reflection of the face merely produces a semblance, yet people, thinking "I have seen my own face," [act accordingly].
They become satisfied through delusion. (Avasam, p.
32–33) Accomplishment (siddhi) is the state of sovereignty over the three realms. (Seṭī, p. 47)
The bliss born from the two organs, which is the crest and the reality, is remembered as the bliss of passionate deities;
the bliss of the Buddhas is imperishable and free from the conduct of the three worlds.
Free from laughter, glances, and the like, devoid of all dualities,
liberated from cause and effect, it is the non-dual manifestation of the three worlds.
Like space, it is non-abiding, all-pervasive, and devoid of defining characteristics;
that is said to be the supreme reality, the unsurpassed vajra-wisdom.
Like space, it is non-abiding, all-pervasive, devoid of characteristics, indefinable, and formless; this is the defining characteristic of reality.
That which is like the pure sky, yet perceived by those clouded by the cataract of ignorance as if covered by moons— such is the reality known by the Victors.
Consecration (*seka*) is for the purpose of washing away the impurity of ignorance, just as external water washes away external impurity. (Seṭī, pp. 58–59)
It is called *seka* because one is sprinkled (*sicyate*) by means of it;
it is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). (Avatāra-saṃgraha, p. 36)
And its very nature is beginningless, unarisen, neither true nor false;
thus, the five aspects that are dependently originated have the nature of the five Tathāgatas.
And because intrinsic nature is non-different from emptiness and compassion,
it is established that the world is non-different from emptiness and compassion;
for, by virtue of its dependent origination, it is clearly like a city of Gandharvas.
The universe does not abide in an intrinsic nature, nor is it like a lotus in the sky.
And it is said in the *Hevajra*: "These very phenomena are nirvāṇa; through delusion, they take the form of saṃsāra. (*Abhisamayamañjarī*, pp. 26–27)
Self-consecration is called "non-consecration," which is the vision of the relative truth. (Seṭī, p.
40) It is the vision of the entire collection of aggregates, elements, and sense-bases as unconstructed, like an illusion, a dream, a city of Gandharvas, a reflected image, and so forth.
The vision of conventional truth is called self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*).
(Seṭī, p. 47) Now, Haṭhayoga is described. Here, when—

Even when the visualized image (*bimba*) has been perfected through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the other stages, the immutable moment (*akṣarakṣaṇa*) does not arise if the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is unrestrained.

At that time, by means of the forceful practice of the *nāda*, one should cause the breath to flow into the central channel; then, through the cessation of the drops of bodhicitta within the vajra-jewel situated at the lotus of wisdom, the immutable moment arises.
"One should accomplish [this] through the motionless" refers to Haṭhayoga;
the practice of *nāda* is taught in this very [work] (*Seṭī*, p.
The syllable *hūṃ* indicates the unsurpassed nature of reality (*dharmatā*) of the middle way; its meaning is as follows: *ha* signifies being free from causes (*hetu*).
"Ū" means free from discursive thought (*ūha*);
"Aṃ" means that all phenomena are without foundation (*apratiṣṭhita*). (Avatamsaka Sutra, p. 37)
